title: Sharks
sources: Florida Museum of Natural History, International Shark Attack File (floridamuseum.ufl.edu)

cover.artAlt: A great white shark gliding calmly through clear, sunlit blue water
cover.blurb: Sharks were swimming here before there were trees. Turn the page and meet them.

pages.title: Rows and Rows of Teeth
pages.artAlt: Close-up of a great white shark swimming peacefully in blue water

facts.text: A shark does not have one row of teeth. It has rows behind rows, like a conveyor belt. When a tooth falls out, the one behind slides forward to take its place, so a shark can go through thousands of teeth in a lifetime.
A shark's skeleton is not made of bone at all. It is made of cartilage, the same bendy stuff inside the tip of your nose. That makes sharks lighter and helps them turn quickly.
facts.artAlt: A shark's jaw and backbone laid out on a museum table, the pale cartilage smooth and rubbery instead of hard white bone
facts.caption: A shark's whole skeleton is bendy cartilage, not bone.

facts.text: Shark skin is covered in tiny tooth-shaped scales called denticles. Rub it one way and it feels like sandpaper, and those scales help water slide past so the shark swims quietly.
facts.artAlt: An extreme close-up of shark skin, covered in rows of tiny overlapping tooth-shaped scales
facts.caption: Up close, shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny teeth.

infographic.title: How many teeth are in there?

rows.label: A great white shark, all its rows

infographic.caption: The shark's 300 teeth, in up to seven rows, come from Smithsonian Ocean. The baby teeth and grown-up teeth are everyday counts, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: The Shark With the Wide, Wide Head
pages.artAlt: A school of hammerhead sharks seen from below against the bright ocean surface

facts.text: A hammerhead's eyes sit at the far ends of its wide head. Spreading them that far apart gives the shark a huge view of the water around it, above and below at the same time.
Scalloped hammerheads gather in big groups called schools, sometimes hundreds of sharks swimming together in slow circles near underwater mountains.
facts.artAlt: A wide view of dozens of scalloped hammerheads circling slowly together in deep blue water
facts.caption: A whole school of hammerheads, turning in slow circles.

facts.text: That wide head is packed with tiny jelly-filled pores that sense electricity. Every living animal gives off a faint electric signal, so a hammerhead can find a fish hiding under the sand without seeing it.
facts.artAlt: A close view of the underside of a hammerhead's wide flat head, dotted all over with tiny dark pores
facts.caption: The little pores that feel a hidden fish's electric buzz.

infographic.title: How a hammerhead finds a fish it cannot see

stops.label: A flat fish hides in the sand with only its eyes showing
Its body gives off a faint electric buzz, as living things do
The wide head sweeps over the sand and feels just where it is

infographic.caption: There are no numbers in this chart, only steps. Hunting a fish buried in the sand comes from the Florida Museum of Natural History.

pages.title: The Biggest Fish in the World
pages.artAlt: A giant spotted whale shark swimming slowly with small striped fish alongside it

facts.text: The whale shark is the largest fish alive today. It can grow longer than a school bus, and it is a shark, not a whale, even though the name says whale.
This giant eats some of the smallest food in the sea. It swims with its mouth open and filters out plankton, tiny drifting plants and animals, plus small fish.
facts.artAlt: A whale shark at the surface with its huge square mouth wide open, cloudy water full of tiny specks pouring in
facts.caption: Mouth wide open, straining the sea for tiny food.

facts.text: Every whale shark has its own pattern of white spots and stripes. Scientists photograph the patterns and use them like fingerprints to tell one shark from another.
facts.artAlt: A close view of the pattern of white spots and pale stripes along a whale shark's dark blue back
facts.caption: No two whale sharks wear the same pattern of spots.

infographic.title: How big is the biggest fish?

rows.label: The biggest whale shark ever measured

infographic.caption: The whale shark's length comes from the Georgia Aquarium and the great white's from the Florida Museum of Natural History. The kid and the school bus are everyday sizes, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: Where Baby Sharks Grow Up
pages.artAlt: A sunny shallow lagoon with several small baby sharks swimming over bright sand

facts.text: A baby shark is called a pup. Many kinds of sharks have their pups in warm, shallow water near mangrove roots and seagrass, a place called a nursery.
Shark pups are on their own from the very first day. Their mother does not stay to feed them, so the shallow nursery keeps them safe from bigger sharks while they grow.
facts.artAlt: One small shark pup swimming by itself through the tangled roots of a mangrove in clear, shallow water
facts.caption: A pup keeps out of trouble among the mangrove roots.

facts.text: Sharks have been swimming in the ocean for more than 400 million years. That is long before the first dinosaurs, and even before the first trees grew on land.
facts.artAlt: A dark, shiny fossil shark tooth resting on a person's open fingertips
facts.caption: A fossil tooth from a shark that swam before the dinosaurs.

infographic.title: Sharks were here first
